2027-03-19.title: Fortieth Friday of the Great Fast · St Joseph, Spouse of the Blessed Virgin Mary
2027-03-19.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-03-19.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). Fortieth Friday (Nalpatham Velli), the sixth Friday of the fast; longer forms in the calendar: Romans 15:1–13; John 11:1–45. St Joseph, Spouse of the Blessed Virgin Mary: Isaiah 41:8–16; Acts 19:11–20; 2 Corinthians 10:3–11; Matthew 1:18–25. In 2027 the two fall on the same day; follow your eparchy's directions on which readings are used and on the penance of the day.
2027-03-19.verse: Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?
theo: Today is the fortieth day since the Great Fast began on Monday 8 February. The Lord fasted forty days in the desert; Moses stayed forty days on the mountain; Elijah walked forty days to Horeb; and the Church, counting with them, keeps this Friday as the Fortieth Friday, Nalpatham Velli. Our forefathers in Kerala called the whole season the fifty-day fast, because it runs on through the Week of the Passion to Easter; the forty days are complete today, and what remains is the road with Christ to Jerusalem. In many parishes the Way of the Cross is made with special devotion today, and some climb a hill shrine on foot, carrying a small cross. In 2027 this day is also the feast of St Joseph, the just man who guarded the Lord's childhood. It is a fitting meeting: the man of silence who obeyed in the night stands at the door of the week in which his foster Son will obey the Father unto death.

The first reading is short and quiet. After the destruction of Sodom, “Abraham went early in the morning to the place where he had stood before the Lord; and he looked down toward Sodom and Gomorrah and toward all the land of the Plain and saw the smoke of the land going up like the smoke of a furnace.” The day before, at that very place, he had bargained with God for the city: fifty righteous, forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten. Not even ten were found. Yet his prayer was not lost: “So it was that, when God destroyed the cities of the Plain, God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow.” No intercession is wasted. The second reading tells of a near civil war. The tribes who had settled east of the Jordan built a great altar by the river, and the other tribes, fearing rebellion and a second altar against the Lord's, gathered at Shiloh to make war. They sent Phinehas and ten chiefs to ask: “What is this treachery that you have committed against the God of Israel?” The rest of the chapter tells that the altar was meant only as a witness that both sides of the river belonged to the one Lord, and war was avoided because they spoke before they fought. Paul gives the Christian rule for every such tension: “Welcome one another, therefore, just as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.” He ends with a blessing worth praying every day of Holy Week: “May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.”

The Gospel brings us to Bethany, to the tomb of Lazarus, the last and greatest sign in John's Gospel before the Passion. “Then Jesus, again greatly disturbed, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone was lying against it. Jesus said, ‘Take away the stone.’” Martha, practical as always, protests: “Lord, already there is a stench because he has been dead four days.” Jesus answers with the word that is today's key: “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?” The stone is rolled away. Jesus lifts his eyes and thanks the Father aloud, “so that they may believe that you sent me.” Then “he cried with a loud voice, ‘Lazarus, come out!’ The dead man came out, his hands and feet bound with strips of cloth, and his face wrapped in a cloth. Jesus said to them, ‘Unbind him, and let him go.’” Lazarus returns to ordinary life and will die again; it is a sign, not yet the Resurrection. But it points to the Easter that is coming, when the stone will be rolled away from another tomb, and the grave cloths will be left lying, because the One who comes out will never die again. Notice too that Jesus gives others a part: they must take away the stone, and they must unbind him. The Church does this still. Christ alone gives life; through the ministry of his Church the bonds of sin are loosed in the sacrament of reconciliation. On this Fortieth Friday, what stone needs to be rolled away, and what bands still hold us?

The readings of St Joseph speak of a man who did not fear. “Do not fear, for I am with you, do not be afraid, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my victorious right hand,” says the Lord through Isaiah. Joseph needed that word. He found the woman he was to marry with child, and “being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her to public disgrace, planned to dismiss her quietly.” Then the angel came in a dream: “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, for the child conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you are to name him Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.” And the Gospel says simply: “When Joseph awoke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him.” Not one word of Joseph is recorded in the Gospels. He speaks through obedience, work and care. He names the child Jesus, “the Lord saves”, and so gives the Son of God his place in the house of David. Pope Francis called him a father in the shadows, and Pope Pius IX declared him Patron of the Universal Church. In many Kerala homes and parishes his feast is marked by a meal for the poor, the oottu, where an elderly man, a woman and a child are honoured at table in memory of the Holy Family of Nazareth. As we enter the Week of the Passion, Joseph teaches us to do what the Lord asks, without speeches, and to trust that “God is with us”, even in the night.
conn: Abraham pleads for Sodom down to ten righteous (Genesis 18:23–32); God remembers him and saves Lot (Genesis 19:29). “The prayer of the righteous is powerful and effective” (James 5:16).

The eastern tribes explain that their altar is not for sacrifice but a witness between them and the other tribes that the Lord is God (Joshua 22:26–29, 34). Speaking first saved Israel from war; Christ is our one altar and our peace (Ephesians 2:14).
Paul quotes Isaiah: “The root of Jesse shall come” (Romans 15:12; Isaiah 11:10). Joseph, son of David, son of Jesse, gives Jesus his legal place in that royal line (Matthew 1:16, 20).

Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones (Ezekiel 37:12–13) is fulfilled first in sign at Bethany and then fully in the Resurrection of Christ and of all who belong to him (John 5:28–29; 1 Corinthians 15:20–23).
Lazarus comes out still bound (John 11:44); at Easter the linen wrappings are left lying in the empty tomb (John 20:6–7), for Christ rises never to die again (Romans 6:9).
Joseph the patriarch, the dreamer, saved his family in Egypt (Genesis 50:20); Joseph of Nazareth, guided by dreams, saved the Saviour by taking him to Egypt and back (Matthew 2:13–15, 19–23).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord who called Lazarus from the tomb gives us his own risen Body, the pledge that he will raise us up on the last day.
Joseph held the Son of God in his arms and fed him with the work of his hands; at every Holy Qurbana the Church receives the same Lord, given to us as the Bread of life.

live: Make the Way of the Cross (Nalpatham Velli)
Walk the stations today, in church or on a hill shrine, offering the forty days of your fast.
Write the names of three people who are far from God and pray for them every day of the Week of the Passion.
Make your Easter confession before Pesaha, and let the Lord loose what binds you.
Share a meal with the poor today, or give for one, in honour of the Holy Family.
fathers: Lazarus four days in the tomb is the soul buried under the habit of sin. When Christ calls, the sinner comes out by confessing; but he comes out still bound, and the Lord says to his ministers, Unbind him: what the Church looses on earth is loosed in heaven.

Joseph is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord set over his household: the comfort of his Mother, the provider for his own humanity, and the one trusted helper in the great work of our salvation. What God gave to the patriarch Joseph, to store bread for a people, he gave to this Joseph, to guard the living Bread from heaven.
magis: Jesus links faith in the resurrection to his own person: “I am the resurrection and the life.” He gives a sign of it by raising the dead, and so announces his own Resurrection.
The raising of Lazarus was a return to ordinary earthly life; Christ's Resurrection is essentially different, for his risen body passes into a life beyond time and space.
Intercession is a prayer of petition that leads us to pray as Jesus did; since Abraham, it belongs to a heart attuned to God's mercy.
Christ chose to be born and grow up in the bosom of the holy family of Joseph and Mary; the Church is nothing other than the family of God.
Joseph is a beloved, tender and obedient father, accepting and creatively courageous, a working father who lived in the shadows; in him Jesus saw the tender love of God.
saints: Fortieth Friday of the Great Fast: the Way of the Cross and, in many places, pilgrimages on foot to hill shrines. Feast of St Joseph, Spouse of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Patron of the Universal Church; in many places a meal for the poor (oottu) in honour of the Holy Family.
2027-03-19.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, resurrection and life, you wept at the tomb of your friend and called him out with a loud voice. On this fortieth day of our fast, roll away the stones that shut us in, call us out of every grave of sin, and let your Church unbind us and set us free. Through the prayers of St Joseph, the just man who did all that the angel commanded, give us his silent obedience and his fearless trust, and bring us with him to the glory of God. To you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory for ever. Amen.

kidsaint: Joseph was a carpenter in Nazareth, the husband of Mary and the foster father of Jesus. He worked hard, protected his family, and took them all the way to Egypt to keep baby Jesus safe. He never says a single word in the Bible, but he always did what God asked. Lesson: you can show your love for God by doing what is right, even without many words!
2027-03-19.special: Fortieth Friday of the Great Fast; feast of St Joseph.
term: The Fortieth Friday: the Friday on which the forty days of the Great Fast are completed, before the road leads on to Hosanna Sunday and the Week of the Passion. It is kept with the Way of the Cross, fasting and pilgrimage.

family.explain: Jesus' friend Lazarus had died and was buried in a cave with a big stone in front. Jesus told the people to move the stone, then he called in a loud voice: “Lazarus, come out!” And Lazarus walked out, alive! Jesus told the others to take off the cloths that were wrapped around him. Jesus has power over death, and at Easter he himself will rise.
family.intention: We pray for fathers today, through St Joseph, and for those who have died.
family.ask: Ask: “Can we do something kind for Appachan today, like St Joseph who cared for his family?”

illus: A carpenter in Kanjirappally kept a small picture of St Joseph above his workbench, with a single line written under it: “He did as the angel commanded.” When his son, newly ordained, asked him why that line and not a prayer, the old man said: “Because in fifty years of work I have found that most of my prayers are answered by the same thing: get up in the morning and do the next right thing God asks.” On his feast the family still feeds three poor neighbours at that bench, an old man, a woman and a child.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you call the dead to life. Call us out of every darkness, through the prayers of St Joseph. Amen.
share: God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow (Genesis 19:29). For whom have I stopped praying?
Welcome one another, therefore, just as Christ has welcomed you (Romans 15:7). Whom do I need to welcome before Easter?
Lazarus, come out! … Unbind him, and let him go (John 11:43–44). What binds me still, and who could help unbind me?
When Joseph awoke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him (Matthew 1:24). What is God asking me to do, simply and without delay?
pm.resp: Lord, you are the resurrection and the life.
interc: For the Church, through the prayers of St Joseph her patron.
For fathers, workers and all who provide for families.
For those buried in sin and despair, that they may hear Christ's voice.
For priests who will hear confessions in these last days of the fast.
For our group, that the forty days may bear fruit at Easter.
pm.close: Father, you remembered Abraham and raised Lazarus through your Son. Give us faith to see your glory, and the obedience of St Joseph to do your will. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today the forty days of the Great Fast are complete. On this Fortieth Friday, and on the feast of St Joseph, the word of God speaks of prayer, peace, life and obedience.

Abraham goes back to the place where he had pleaded with God for Sodom and sees only smoke. But Scripture says: God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow (Genesis 19:29). No prayer for another person is ever wasted.

When the tribes east of the Jordan built an altar, the rest of Israel almost went to war. But they spoke first, and the misunderstanding was healed. Paul tells us: welcome one another, therefore, just as Christ has welcomed you (Romans 15:7).

At the tomb of Lazarus, Jesus says: take away the stone. Martha fears the stench of death. Jesus answers: did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God? (John 11:40). Then he cries: Lazarus, come out! And he tells the people: unbind him, and let him go.

Christ alone gives life; through his Church he unbinds us. In these days, let us come to the sacrament of reconciliation and let the bands of sin be loosed. Lazarus points to Easter, when Christ will rise never to die again.

St Joseph never speaks in the Gospels. When the angel told him in a dream not to be afraid, he woke up and did as the angel of the Lord commanded (Matthew 1:24). As we enter the Week of the Passion, let us learn from him to obey without delay and to trust that God is with us. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus called out loud to his friend Lazarus who had died: Lazarus, come out! And he came out alive! Jesus is stronger than death.
Today we also remember St Joseph, who took care of Jesus and Mary. Let us help our fathers and mothers today, just as St Joseph helped his family.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the Gospel gives St Joseph only one description: Joseph, being a righteous man (Matthew 1:19). In the Bible a righteous man is one who lives in right relationship with God and with others. Let us look at what Joseph's righteousness looked like.

When he learned that Mary was with child, and before he knew the angel's message, he was unwilling to expose her to public disgrace and planned to dismiss her quietly. His justice was not cold. It protected the weak and refused to shame anyone. Micah said that God asks us to do justice, to love kindness and to walk humbly (Micah 6:8). Joseph did all three.

Then came the night of danger. The angel said: get up, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt (Matthew 2:13). Joseph got up, took the child and his mother by night and went. He was the guardian of the Redeemer and of his Mother, not their owner. Like Joseph of old in Egypt, through whose hands God saved lives, our Joseph served God's plan by his care.

And in Nazareth, people later asked about Jesus: is not this the carpenter's son? (Matthew 13:55). For years Joseph worked with wood and tools, earned bread for his family and taught Jesus his trade. God gave man the garden to till and keep (Genesis 2:15). Through Joseph, ordinary work became holy.

Today, near the end of the Great Fast, let us ask St Joseph for a just heart: merciful to those who are accused, brave to protect our families, faithful in our daily work. Let us offer our work each morning through him, and receive his Son at the Holy Qurbana with the love with which Joseph held him. Amen.

opts.a: Joseph and the hope of a holy death
intro: St Joseph is honoured as patron of a holy death, because, as tradition holds, he died in the presence of Jesus and Mary. The Gospel of this Fortieth Friday, the raising of Lazarus, speaks of the same hope.

sub: Not one word of his is recorded.
points.apply: Keep five minutes of silence before the Lord each day of Holy Week.

homily: Dear friends, the Gospels do not record a single word of St Joseph. Yet the Church honours him above all the saints after the Virgin Mary. His silence was not emptiness; it was a listening heart. Lamentations says: it is good that one should wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD (Lamentations 3:26).

God spoke to Joseph in the night. Four times God spoke to him in a dream, and each time he rose and obeyed. After Herod's death the angel said: get up, take the child and his mother, and go to the land of Israel, and he got up and went (Matthew 2:20–21). Like Jacob who saw a ladder in the night and woke saying, surely the LORD is in this place (Genesis 28:16), Joseph found God in the dark.

The Gospel of this Fortieth Friday takes us to the tomb of Lazarus. Jesus said to Martha: I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live (John 11:25). Then he called: Lazarus, come out! What Ezekiel had seen in vision, God opening the graves of his people, began at Bethany and will be complete on the last day.

An ancient and pious tradition tells us that Joseph died before Jesus began his public ministry, with Jesus and Mary at his side. That is why we call him the patron of a holy death. What better way to die than in the arms of Jesus and his Mother? This is the death we pray for, and the death we pray for others to receive.

So on this feast, at the threshold of Holy Week, let us learn Joseph's silence, trust God in our nights, and pray each evening for the dying. And let us ask St Joseph to obtain for us the grace to die, when our hour comes, with the name of Jesus and Mary on our lips, strengthened by the Holy Qurbana. Amen.
